cases.user_message: Привет! Дочка поступила в вуз, хочу подарить ей ноутбук. Бюджет до 90 тысяч рублей, можно чуть больше если реально стоит того. Что посоветуешь взять? Хочу заказать на этой неделе, пока скидки.
cases.why_in_scope: The request hides the facts that decide the purchase: what she is studying (design or programming versus humanities), whether she needs Windows or would take a Mac, and how often she will carry it. The component makes the model ask a few targeted questions and restate its understanding before recommending anything. A strong model without it usually lists 3-5 'universal' models built on guesses it doesn't mention, and the list may suit the wrong major.
rubric: Asks at most 3 specific clarifying questions, and they target the deciding unknowns (e.g. field of study or software she will run, OS preference or constraint, portability/battery needs), not generic filler
Restates its understanding of the request in its own words (gift for a first-year student, budget around 90k RUB with some flexibility, order this week) and invites correction
Does not present a final specific-model recommendation as if the unknowns were settled; any preliminary direction is clearly labelled as depending on the answers

Stays practical for a parent ordering this week: explains briefly why the answers matter (e.g. they narrow the choice quickly) and any preliminary pointers are realistic for a ~90k RUB budget, without a long generic buyer's guide

cases.user_message: Can you write me a PRD for adding notifications to our product? Context: we're a B2B SaaS for dental clinics in the US, ~400 clinics on the platform, front desk staff and dentists use it daily for scheduling and charting. Leadership just said "we need notifications" in the quarterly review and I have to bring something to sprint planning on Monday.
cases.why_in_scope: "Notifications" could mean patient-facing appointment reminders over SMS/email, in-app alerts for clinic staff, or both, and each one leads to a very different PRD with its own scope, compliance exposure and success metrics. The component makes the model ask a few targeted questions and confirm its reading before drafting. A strong model without it usually writes a full PRD for whichever reading it picks, and that PRD may not match what leadership meant.
rubric: Surfaces the core ambiguity explicitly: who receives the notifications (patients vs clinic staff) and via which channels, and asks about it rather than silently choosing

Asks no more than 3 targeted questions, which may include the business problem behind leadership's request (e.g. no-shows, missed tasks) or success metric, and restates its understanding for the user to confirm or correct
If patient-facing messaging is on the table, flags that it involves patient health information and HIPAA considerations for US clinics

Does not deliver a complete PRD built on unstated assumptions; any skeleton or outline offered is explicitly conditional, and the reply respects the Monday deadline (e.g. says a draft can follow quickly once the answers are in)

checker_notes: Both cases are in scope (underspecified requests where strong models typically answer on silent assumptions), leak-free, tool-less, and use owner agents. Only change: made case 1's last rubric item a clearer general-quality check (realistic pointers for the budget, why answers matter) instead of vague conciseness; HIPAA item in case 2 verified as correct and kept.
